title: The Concept of Victory
paragraphs: We can achieve victory by either vying with others or by striving on our own. Vākai does not refer only to the victory achieved in war. In fact, it is the attaining of a lofty goal in life through virtuous means.
Tolkāppiyam, Poruḷatikāram explains the classifications of vākai as well as its defining traits and its grammar.

That verse in question begins thus, “The sixfold occupations of the brahmins,” After reading it, one might feel like wondering, “What exactly is this Brahmin occupation? How on earth did brahmins appear in Tolkāppiyam?”
They had indeed arrived but their arrival was portended in Collatikāram itself. Somehow, the Tamiḻs had lost sight of the fact that the sound of the bell would signal the advent of the elephant.
In the cultivated fields weeds grow along with crop unannounced. Tolkāppiyam touches upon that in the verse below:

> Vaṭacol comprises words (borrowed from Sanskrit) > That steer clear of the system of sounds in Sanskrit > And that come to be adapted to the native form and sound. > > (Collatikāram : Ecca iyal, verse 5)
How many years ago was the door kept open for this phenomenon?

Researchers fix Tolkāppiyam to the seventh century B.C. That is, approximately 2500 years ago, Sanskrit smelt the favoured environment and the way was paved for the entry of the Aryans into the Tamiḻ land.
This verse in vākaittiṇai attests to their entrenchment.

> The seven modes of vocations > Which the theme of vākai celebrates are: > The sixfold occupations of the brahmins > [Learning, instruction, performing sacrifices, > Making others perform sacrifices, > Munificence and being beneficiaries of munificence]; > The fivefold occupations of the kings > [Learning, performing sacrifices, munificence, > Protecting the country and administering justice]; > The sixfold occupations of the other [tradesmen and cultivating] classes > [Learning, farming, trading, rearing cattle, > Forms of worship and acts of liberality]; > The calling of sages and astrologers - > The flawless reading of planetary movements > In relation to their effects on the past, present and future -- > The eightfold functions of ascetics > [Bathing, lying on the bare ground, > Wearing leather covering, consecrated fire worship, > Keeping away from habitations of people, > Keeping undressed hair, > Eating forest produce and worshipping god]; > The demarcated skills of excellence of the warrior class; > And the myriad callings other than the above > [Such as music, drama and singing]. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Puṟattiṇai iyal, verse 20)

The expression “so said the poets,” clearly indicates the Aryan arrival, either during Tolkāppiyar’s time, or even earlier. They had stamped their hold on our land and people, along with their codes of living which were alien to the Tamiḻ mores.

According to Tolkāppiyar, Brahmins had six duties - to chant mantras , make others chant mantras , conduct homams, make others conduct homams, to give and to accept gifts. The king’s five cardinal duties were - to chant mantras, to conduct homams, to give gifts, to offer army’s support to allies, and to protect the subjects. The traders and peasants had six duties - to chant mantras, to conduct homams, to give gifts, to cultivate, to trade and to maintain the livestock. To calculate and monitor the events of the three times, namely, the past, the present, and the future, was the duty of persons endowed with wisdom. The recluse had the duties of upholding eight types of discipline. While being aware of these duties, the army leaders’ duty was to accomplish victory, not only through the might of sword or arms, but also through the means of these duties. Such a victory was supposed to be more enduring.

Though many of these duties underlined could uplift one’s stature of life, the two duties of conducting homams, and making others follow the practice of conducting homams provided opportunities for the Brahmins and such people to resort to discrimination which was completely alien to the Tamiḻ land.
Vēṭal means to conduct homams, while vēṭpittal is to make others conduct homams.
The practice of offering sacrifice and conducting homams crept into the Tamiḻ land through the wiles of the Brahmins.

It took roots and branched out among the Tamiḻs thanks to the cleverness of the brahmins. Victory could be amassed through bravery which required waging wars and perseverance. Real victory in life and happiness could be achieved by getting involved in various virtuous deeds, even cutting across national boundaries. What then was the necessity for these unavailing practices of conducting homams and offering sacrifices? There would have been reservations and protests. But would the priestly class allow this to be given up?
If the subtle manipulation combined with versatile abilities worked, it was natural that even an emperor would be hypnotized in the meandering smoke of camphor.
Therefore, conducting homams and the practice of making others conduct homams started slowly but gained momentum of a forest flood and breached the banks.

Those who wielded arms like spear, sword, lance and trident and rode on horses and those who sang of the power of love and the breathlike passion for the motherland had to stoop before the fire pit of the homam, prostrate and remain in a hunched posture to drink the urine of cow, in keeping with the practice of conducting homams.

Even that great Cēraṉ Ceṅkuṭṭuvaṉ of Cilappatikāram who successfully led the Himalayan campaign and brought the stone for carving the statue of Kaṇṇaki on the heads of the northern kings Kaṉakaṉ and Vicayaṉ had to fall in line.
That renowned warrior was beaten squarely by the vedic rites and rituals.

The invasion followed by the bringing of stone for the Kaṇṇaki statue was over. Kaṉaka-Vicayaṉ were also imprisoned. At that juncture, a person of the Aryan priestly class, Māṭala Maṟaiyōṉ, met the king and offered advice, which bore fruit. The kings of northern origin were set free. In keeping with the advice of the priest, the king made preparations for a homam. That work was entrusted to the army chief Villavaṉkōtai:

> You, master of wisdom, listen to my words: > Vedic sacrifices prescribed for kings > You need to perform with priestly cooperation: > This will surely lead you to salvation, > That would gladden heavenly beings. > If you postpone it for tomorrow, who knows > For certain his last day? Supppose....”

> Māṭalaṉ prayed for long life to the king, > His consort, and the brave king kneeling > Before him; he did sow thoughts of higher being > In the mind of Kuṭṭuvaṉ, the Cēra king. > The sowing resulted in abundant harvest; > The valiant king, eager to enjoy the best, > Engaged priests, who had studied the vedas, > And had all doubts cleared by their gurus, > To perform the sacrificial rites to conform > To the wise Māṭalaṉ’s prescription.

> He released the Aryan kings from prison, > And lodged them in Velāvikkō mansion > Outside the city walls, and surrounded > By shady groves; he announced their freedom > To go home, after the sacrifices were concluded. > He instructed Villavaṉkōtai to show due courtesy to them.
In his elucidation of Tolkāppiyam, Nāvalar Cōmacuntara Pāratiyār categorically rejects the presence of caste-based classification of Akattiṇai iyal and Puṟattiṇai iyal.

The great scholar Veḷḷaivāraṇar subscribes to this view in his Tolkāppiyam studies and says: “The four types of caste observed in books of northern origin were unheard of among the ancient Tamiḻ people.” This was his categorical averment. He adds, “The practice of classifying people on the basis of caste was never prevalent in the ancient Tamiḻ country. The categorization was only on the basis of the geographical regions they inhabited.” Though these two learned academics claim so, it cannot be denied that the custom of classifying people on the basis of caste sneaked in either overtly or covertly and got established firmly.
In came castes to begin homams and sacrifices heralding the advent of the Brahmins in vākaittiṇai itself.
If one were to put it with a tinge of sadness, it would be rather more appropriate to describe vākaittiṇai as the ‘tiṇai of the Aryan advent’.
